title: Chapter 27 — The Lifestyle Demo
intro: A demonstration is not a feature tour. It is the moment you connect what you learned in discovery to the product standing in front of the customer. Show them their life — not a spec sheet.

sections.title: The Demo Is Not About the Product
sections.content:
Most salespeople think a demonstration means walking someone through every feature on the appliance. Open this door, look at this shelf, see this light, check out this drawer.

That is a feature tour. It is not a demonstration.

A real demonstration connects the features that matter to the customer's actual life. You learned what matters during discovery. Now you show them why this specific product solves their specific problem and fits the way they actually live.

The difference sounds like this:

Feature tour: 'This refrigerator has flexible shelving that adjusts to six positions.'

Lifestyle demo: 'You mentioned you entertain a lot and need room for large platters. Watch this — these shelves fold back flat so you can fit a full party tray without rearranging everything. No more playing Tetris the night before a dinner party.'

Same feature. Completely different impact. One informs. The other sells.

sections.title: Solve the Need First
sections.content:
Step 4 of the 10 Steps is Needs Assessment. By the time you reach the demonstration, you should already know what this product must do.

Every recommendation must first satisfy the customer's needs. Needs are functional — keep food cold, fit the space, stay within budget, get delivered on time. Without meeting them, your recommendation fails.

Start your demonstration by confirming the needs are handled. 'This is a 36-inch counter-depth model, so it fits your existing cabinet opening. It is in stock and we can have it delivered by Thursday. And it comes in right at the budget range you mentioned.'

That takes thirty seconds. But it tells the customer: I listened. I found something that works. Now let me show you why you are going to love it.

That is the transition from needs to wants.

sections.title: Sell the Want
sections.content:
Step 5 is Wants Assessment. This is where the demonstration becomes exciting — for the customer and for you.

Wants answer the question: 'What would make ownership enjoyable?' French doors, ice dispensers, fingerprint-resistant finishes, quiet operation, soft-close drawers, smart features, designer appearance.

People rarely become excited about buying what they need. They become excited about buying what they want. Every refrigerator keeps food cold. That is why refrigerators exist. Very few customers buy a particular refrigerator simply because it keeps food cold. They buy it because it fits the way they live, the way they entertain, the way they cook — or because every morning they will enjoy using it.

During the demo, connect every want you uncovered to a feature on the product. Make it physical — open the doors, pull out the drawers, turn on the lights. Let them touch it. Let them interact with it. The more real it feels, the more they can picture it in their home.

sections.title: Never Skip the Demo
sections.content:
Even when you are convinced you have already found the perfect solution, complete the demonstration. Here is why.

A proper demonstration builds confidence. Confidence reduces objections. Reduced objections increase closing rates.

You know what you are talking about. But your customer does not shop for appliances every day. What feels obvious to you may be completely new to them. They need to understand why it is the right choice — not just hear you say it is.

The demo is Step 7 in the 10 Steps — Presentation. Skipping it means jumping from recommendation straight to close. That is like a doctor prescribing medication and then handing you a bill without explaining what it does or why you need it. It might be the right answer, but you do not feel confident about it.

The demo gives the customer the confidence to say yes.

sections.title: When Words Are Not Enough — Use Video
sections.content:
Some products need to be experienced. But not every customer can come into the store. They are busy, they have children, they have long commutes, or there are multiple decision-makers who cannot all visit at the same time.

Instead of asking the customer to drive to the store, bring the showroom to them.

Use Google Meet, Zoom, FaceTime, WhatsApp — any secure video platform the customer is comfortable using. Walk to the product with your phone. Then perform the exact same demonstration you would perform standing beside them.

Show them the exterior design, the interior layout, the shelving, the drawers, the controls, the finishes, the lighting, the unique features. The customer should feel like they are standing beside you.

This also solves what I call the Scout Problem. Many purchases involve more than one decision-maker. Often one person gathers information while the other approves the purchase. That creates 'I will come back with my spouse.' Video removes that friction. Invite the second decision-maker into the call. Sell to everyone at once. Questions answered immediately. Objections handled together. The buying journey becomes shorter and more collaborative.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating a salesperson's demonstration, ask:

Did they connect product features to the customer's specific needs and wants — or just list features?
Did they confirm the functional needs were met before moving to wants?
Did they let the customer interact with the product physically?
Did they complete a full demonstration even when the solution seemed obvious?
Did they offer a video demonstration when the customer or a decision-maker could not be present?
Did the customer leave the demo feeling more confident than when they arrived?

The best demos do not sell features. They sell the customer's future life with the product in it.
